text: Neuroimaging and patient studies of 'mental time travel' (remembering the past and imagining the future) most strongly support which conclusion?
choices: Future imagination is handled by prefrontal cortex alone, while episodic memory is handled by the hippocampus alone
Imagining the future is simply episodic memory run in reverse, drawing on no shared neural machinery
Both draw on a shared 'core network' including the hippocampus, so hippocampal damage impairs both episodic recall and vivid future imagining
Only humans can represent the past, whereas future planning is widely shared across mammals and has no special neural basis
explanation: Studies converge on a shared 'core network' — notably the hippocampus, medial prefrontal, posterior cingulate, and lateral temporal-parietal regions — active in both episodic recollection and future imagining; patients with hippocampal damage (Hassabis et al. 2007) produce sparse, fragmented imagined future scenes as well as impaired memory, indicating a common 'scene construction' capacity. Choice 1 wrongly segregates the two into separate regions; choice 2 denies the shared machinery (the book stresses future imagining is not merely memory 'in reverse'); choice 4 garbles the comparative-cognition debate, in which food-caching corvids are candidate non-human mental time travelers.
